title: UNICEF Says the Iran War Is Now Delaying Lifesaving Aid to Children by Up to Six Months
excerpt: Surging transport costs, port congestion, and shipping reroutes have nearly exhausted the agency's annual flight donations in a single quarter — with the Ebola response in Congo adding to the strain.
body:
The Iran war is no longer just an oil crisis. It is now a children's health crisis.

Nearly 100 days into the conflict, the United Nations children's agency UNICEF warned on Tuesday that surging transport costs, fuel prices, and congestion at alternative ports have delayed the delivery of lifesaving medical supplies to some of the world's most vulnerable children by up to six months.

## Air Freight Budgets Exhausted in One Quarter

The numbers are stark. UNICEF said it had nearly exhausted its entire annual allocation of donated charter flights in just the first quarter of 2026 — flying supplies into Lebanon and Gaza as shipping delays stretched to four to six weeks. Jean-Cedric Meeus, UNICEF's Chief of Global Transport and Logistics, called the pace of air freight spending unprecedented.

The agency is also relying heavily on air transport to respond to the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda, as East African ports in Mombasa and Dar es Salaam remain congested from the global rerouting of maritime traffic.

Rerouting shipments around the Cape of Good Hope — the primary detour since the Strait of Hormuz closure — adds two to four weeks to delivery times and has pushed insurance premiums sharply higher.

## The Human Cost in Numbers

UNICEF's transport budget in Mali surged 36% in the first quarter alone. The agency said it was now forced to choose between scaling back shipments of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food — the calorie-dense packets that keep malnourished children alive — or cutting water and sanitation programmes.

The cost of trucking those food cartons from Kenyan manufacturers to Somalia, South Sudan, and the DRC has risen 30%. A polio vaccination campaign in Nigeria required an additional $200,000 just for rerouted syringe deliveries — a 56% spike in transport costs for a single shipment.

## India's Role in the Global Vaccine Chain

The disruption carries particular significance for the Indian diaspora and India's global health footprint. India manufactures roughly 60% of the world's vaccines, and its Serum Institute is a primary supplier to Gavi, the global vaccine alliance. Supply chain bottlenecks that delay delivery of Indian-made vaccines to Africa and the Middle East ripple back to India's pharmaceutical export economy.

The same day UNICEF issued its warning, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Congress that Washington would re-engage with Gavi after pulling its $300 million annual funding last year under pressure from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. India has separately pledged $20 million to Gavi's 2026-2030 strategic cycle.

## A War with No Frontline for Children

The Iran conflict's impact on children's health extends well beyond the Middle East. From malnourished toddlers in South Sudan waiting for therapeutic food packets to infants in Nigeria awaiting polio vaccines, the supply chain disruptions have created a shadow crisis — one without explosions or headlines, but with consequences measured in lives.

UNICEF's appeal was blunt: the war may be fought with missiles and drones, but its collateral damage is being tallied in months of delayed medicine, rising trucking bills, and children who cannot wait.
author: Diaspora Desk
